sections.executive_summary:
### Opportunity snapshot
In New York, any agency that provides **personal care, home health aide or nursing services** in a client's home must hold a **Licensed Home Care Services Agency (LHCSA)** license under Public Health Law Article 36 [S1]. The Public Health and Health Planning Council (PHHPC) approves each license; DOH issues it after a pre-opening survey [S3].

**New applications are being accepted.** The 2018–2020 moratorium expired on March 31, 2020 [S3]. DOH reopened filing with a new application in August 2022 (DAL 22-14) [S4][S8]. No moratorium is in effect in October 2026. A bill to impose a new moratorium from April 1, 2027 to March 31, 2029 (S4400) sits in the Senate Health Committee and has not passed [S9].

**But public need is the gate.** Since April 1, 2020, every new LHCSA must prove public need, financial feasibility and character and competence [S1][S2]. There is a rebuttable **presumption of no need** in any county that already has **five or more LHCSAs each actively serving at least 25 patients** [S2][S3]. In DOH's latest published survey (2022), **20 counties** were on the no-need list. They include all five NYC counties, Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester, Erie, Monroe, Onondaga and Albany. The other **42 counties** had presumed need [S5]. In a no-need county you must file a data-driven rebuttal, county by county, or DOH will not accept the application [S3].

### What drives profit
- **Wage floors.** Home care aides earn at least **$19.65** an hour downstate and **$18.65** upstate in 2026. Those rise to $20.00 / $19.00 on January 1, 2027 [S14][S16]. Medicaid work in NYC, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester also carries **wage parity** benefits of $2.54 (NYC) or $1.67 an hour [S17].
- **Payers.** Most Medicaid personal care flows through **MLTC plans** (338,186 enrollees, $15.7 billion in 2022) [S32]. Plans negotiate rates privately. The only published benchmark is DOH's **$32.11/hour** NYC FFS Level II rate, effective January 1, 2024 [S19].
- **Private pay.** The New York median for non-medical in-home care is **$35/hour** [S36].

**Bottom line from the model.** An **upstate (presumed-need county) agency** works. An agency with 80 clients, 65% MLTC Medicaid and 35% private pay, nets about **$25,000 a month (12.3%)** at 90% census, *if* plans pay near the $32.11 benchmark. A Medicaid-only upstate agency with 60 clients nets about $20,400. It breaks even at about **$28.33/hour**. **Downstate** is much harder. A 100-client NYC Medicaid agency loses about $7,050 a month at $32.11 once parity pay and the MCTMT payroll tax are included, and needs about **$32.89/hour** to break even. Downstate counties also start with a presumption of no need.
sections.service_model:
### What the license covers
New York uses one license type for non-medical and paraprofessional home care: the **Licensed Home Care Services Agency (LHCSA)**. Since 1986, PHL §3605 has required a license for any agency that provides **nursing, home health aide or personal care services**, directly or by contract [S1]. Exemptions are narrow. They cover agencies serving clients only through another state agency's program, licensed nurses' registries and sole practitioners [S1].

DOH defines **personal care services** as "assistance to the patient with personal hygiene, dressing, feeding and household tasks essential to his/her health" [S28]. Medicaid splits personal care into two levels [S23]:
- **Level I** covers nutritional and environmental support only (meals, cleaning, laundry, shopping), capped at 8 hours a week.
- **Level II** adds hands-on help with bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring and feeding.

A LHCSA may also employ **home health aides**, who perform health-related tasks under RN supervision [S28].

**Companion-only care.** A business that provides only companionship, with no hands-on care and no household tasks essential to health, may fall outside the license requirement, because §3605 lists only nursing, home health aide and personal care [S1]. The line is fine, though. Housekeeping "essential to health" is part of the personal care definition [S28]. Get DOH's written view before operating unlicensed, and assume a license is needed the moment aides help with any ADL.

**LHCSA vs. CHHA.** A LHCSA does not bill Medicare. Medicare home health requires a separate Certified Home Health Agency, which is outside this bundle.

### Who is served
- Older adults and adults with disabilities who need help with ADLs.
- Medicaid recipients authorized for personal care by their MLTC plan or local district.
- Private-pay families.

New York had 20.0 million residents in 2025, and 19.3% were aged 65+ [S34].

### Regulatory framework
- **Licensure:** PHL Article 36 [S1]; 10 NYCRR Part 765 (establishment, review standards, public need) [S6][S2].
- **Operations:** 10 NYCRR Part 766 (patient rights, plan of care, governing authority, personnel) [S27][S24][S25][S26].
- **Medicaid personal care:** 18 NYCRR §505.14 [S23].
- **Workforce:** Home Care Registry and criminal history record checks (CHRC) under 10 NYCRR Parts 403 and 402 [S26][S29]. Wages are set by PHL §3614-f (minimum wage) and §3614-c (wage parity) [S14][S17].
- **CDPAP** is a separate consumer-directed program. Since 2025, **Public Partnerships LLC (PPL)** has been the single Statewide Fiscal Intermediary, and all CDPAP consumers must use PPL [S30]. A LHCSA cannot use CDPAP as a revenue line. Families who leave CDPAP and want agency care are a possible referral source.
sections.licensing_pathway:
### Step 1 — Check public need for your counties first
Decide your service counties before anything else.
- **Limits:** An initial license covers up to **5 counties**, all in one DOH region. One county may be in a neighboring region if it is contiguous [S3].
- **Need test:** Each county is its own planning area [S2]. If 5+ LHCSAs actively serve 25+ patients there, need is presumed absent [S2][S3].
- **2022 no-need counties (20) [S5]:** Albany, Bronx, Broome, Chautauqua, Dutchess, Erie, Kings, Monroe, Nassau, New York, Onondaga, Orange, Putnam, Queens, Richmond, Rockland, Saratoga, Suffolk, Ulster and Westchester.
- **Presumed need (42) [S5]:** All other counties, for example Oneida, Niagara, Schenectady, Rensselaer, Jefferson, Ontario, Steuben, St. Lawrence, Sullivan, Tompkins and Warren.

The list comes from a 2022 survey. DOH has collected weekly patient census by licensed county through HERDS since June 2025 [S43], so confirm current status with DOH before filing.

**Rebuttal.** A rebuttal must use the §765-1.16(d) factors, with data for each no-need county [S2][S3]:
- demographics and health status;
- documented, unduplicated waiting lists;
- the capacity and quality of existing agencies;
- workforce availability and training resources;
- cultural competency;
- specialty subpopulations.

Every applicant must also agree to serve groups that have trouble getting care because of minority status, age, case complexity, payment source or geography [S2].

**Exemptions.** These routes skip the need test [S2][S3]:
- buying an existing LHCSA that actively serves **25+ patients** (a change of ownership);
- an agency affiliated with an ALP, PACE, Nurse-Family Partnership or CCRC, restricted to that program's patients.

### Step 2 — Assemble the application
The application is filed electronically in **NYSE-CON** [S3]. Reviewers look at three things [S6][S7]:
- **Character and competence.** Schedule 1 disclosures cover every principal. At least one principal must have health care experience. The application lists all U.S. health care facilities you have controlled, with any enforcement history.
- **Financial feasibility.** You need documented **working capital of at least two months of estimated operating expenses**, a reasonableness test on start-up funding, and projections showing revenue meets or exceeds expenses over time. Loans count only if awarded and documented at filing. A **CPA** must review the funding [S6][S3][S4].
- **Public need** (Step 1).

### Step 3 — Pay the fee
The fee is **$2,000** (PHL §3605(13)). The check is payable to the NYS Department of Health, marked with the NYSE-CON submission number, and due **within 30 days of submission** [S1][S3]. It is nonrefundable once DOH acknowledges the application, including if PHHPC disapproves it [S3].

### Step 4 — DOH review and PHHPC
- DOH reviews applications in the order they are acknowledged and may send requests for information [S3].
- The application then goes on a **PHHPC agenda**. PHHPC meets **six times a year** [S3].
- PHHPC may approve, contingently approve or disapprove. It can propose disapproval on public need alone, before the other reviews are finished [S2].
- DOH publishes no processing time [S3].

### Step 5 — After contingent approval
1. Submit your **Policy & Procedure Manual** to the regional home care office [S3][S4].
2. Pass the **pre-opening survey** [S3].
3. The regional office recommends licensure, and the Bureau of Home Care Licensure and Certification issues the license [S3].

### Step 6 — Before billing
- **Register annually** under PHL §3605-b. This has been required since January 1, 2019. Unregistered agencies cannot operate or be paid. The late penalty is $500 a month, and missing two registration periods can lead to revocation [S13].
- **Medicaid:** enroll as a Medicaid provider and sign MLTC plan contracts. A new agency that wants a FFS rate files a **Budgeted Projections Statement** [S22].
- **EVV:** set up a compliant EVV system [S31].

### Changes after licensure
- Adding counties, services or sites is handled administratively through the regional office (homecareapplications@health.ny.gov) [S3]. Counties remain subject to the need rule.
- A license cannot be transferred. A new owner needs a full application and receives a new license number [S3].
sections.reimbursement:
### How money flows
**1. Medicaid managed long term care (MLTC) — the main Medicaid channel.**
- Plans received $15.7 billion in premiums for 338,186 enrollees in 2022 [S32].
- An LHCSA contracts with each plan and bills the plan at a **negotiated hourly rate**. No public MLTC rate schedule exists.
- Plans must keep at least two LHCSAs accepting new enrollees in every county [S12].
- DOH's 2018 guidance also **caps how many LHCSAs a partial-cap plan may contract with**: 1 per 100 enrollees downstate and 1 per 60 rest of state, from October 1, 2019 [S12]. A new agency may find plans' networks full. Whether the caps are still enforced in 2026 was not verified (see "not claimed").

**2. Medicaid fee-for-service (FFS).**
- **NYC:** DOH sets uniform rates for agencies under NYC HRA contracts. Effective January 1, 2024: Level II **$32.11**, Level I $32.64, Hard to Serve $32.16 [S18][S19].
- **Rest of state:** rates are provider-specific and built from cost reports. CY2024 Level II rates mostly fall between about $30 and $41 [S20].
- The latest FFS rates (CY2024) were released March 17, 2026 and take effect for payment in eMedNY in April 2026 [S21].
- A new agency without cost history needs a **budgeted rate** via the Budgeted Projections Statement [S22].
- The FFS book is small because most adults needing ongoing personal care are enrolled in MLTC.

**3. Private pay.** The New York median is **$35/hour** for non-medical in-home care [S36]. This is a statewide median of agency rates. Downstate prices are likely higher, but no citable figure was found.

**4. CDPAP is not available to agencies.** PPL is the sole fiscal intermediary [S30].

### Eligibility changes affecting volume
From **September 1, 2025**, Medicaid applicants age 21+ seeking personal care or CDPAS must need at least limited assistance with physical maneuvering with **more than two ADLs**. For people with dementia or Alzheimer's, the standard is supervision with more than one ADL. DOH states the requirement "applies to initial assessments and subsequent reassessment that occurred on or after September 1, 2025," and also applies to Medicaid recipients **18+** who want to enroll in an MLTC or Medicaid Advantage Plus (MAP) plan [S30].

Authorizations rest on an independent assessment and a practitioner order, completed at least annually. No authorization lasts longer than 12 months [S23].

### Wage-driven costs built into rates
- **Home care aide minimum wage [S14][S16]:**
  - 2026: $19.65 downstate / $18.65 upstate;
  - 2027: $20.00 / $19.00.
- DOH tells MLTC plans that their capitation assumes they pay **$0.55 more per hour** of home care from January 1, 2026, and that the requirement applies to all payer types [S44]. Cite this when negotiating, because contracts do not automatically raise your rate; negotiate wage-increase language into every MLTC contract.
- **Wage parity** applies to Medicaid-funded aides in NYC, Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester [S17]:
  - NYC: aide minimum + **$2.54** benefit portion = **$22.19** total compensation in 2026;
  - Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester: + **$1.67** = **$21.32**.
- Parity work requires an annual certification and an independently audited statement. Government payers may not pay for care delivered by underpaid aides [S17].

### Billing mechanics
- Medicaid personal care requires EVV, with data sent to the NYS EVV Data Aggregator. PCS compliance was due January 1, 2021 [S31].
- Payment requires a valid annual registration [S13].
- Billing codes and units differ by MLTC plan. Confirm them in each contract.

- **MLTC enrollment** roughly doubled from **174,453 (2015)** to **329,618 (2020)** [S33]. It stood at **338,186** in 2022, with $15.7 billion in premiums [S32].
- **Workforce scale:** New York employs **663,140** home health and personal care aides, more than in most entire state health workforces [S35].
- **Aging:** 19.3% of New York's 20.0 million residents are aged 65+ [S34].
- **Private-pay purchasing power:** median household income is $85,974 [S34]. At the $35 median rate [S36], 20 hours a week costs about $3,030 a month.

### Headwinds for new Medicaid volume
- **Stricter eligibility.** The September 1, 2025 Minimum Needs Requirements (more than two ADLs) narrow who newly qualifies for personal care and MLTC [S30].
- **Saturated counties.** The need rule exists because DOH found many counties already well served. Twenty counties, covering most of the population, had 5+ agencies each serving 25+ patients in 2022 [S5].
- **Plan networks.** MLTC contract caps may keep plans from adding agencies [S12].

### Referral sources
- **MLTC plan care managers.** Your contract decides whether you receive cases.
- **NYC HRA and local districts** for the remaining FFS cases [S18].
- **Hospital and rehab discharge planners, physicians, elder law attorneys and senior centers** for private pay.
- **Former CDPAP consumers** who want an agency instead of self-direction after the PPL transition [S30].

### Where to locate
The economics and the need rule both point **upstate, to presumed-need counties** [S5]. These have smaller incumbent networks, lower wage floors and no wage parity. Within a 5-county initial license, choose counties in one DOH region [S3].
sections.operations:
### Required leadership and staffing
- **Governing authority** is responsible for compliance, policies, an adequately sized office and enough staff [S25].
- **RN:** the agency must employ at least one licensed RN to direct and supervise patient care [S25].
- **Quality improvement committee:** must include a consumer and health professionals, and meet at least **four times a year** to review policies and a sample of records [S25].
- **Complaints:** keep a complaint log and respond in writing within **15 days**. Appeals go to the governing authority within 30 days [S25].
- **Emergency plan** to keep care going during disruptions [S25].
- **24-hour emergency contacts** listed in the Health Provider Network directory [S25].
- **Management or franchise contracts** need commissioner approval, submitted 60 days in advance [S25].

### Aide qualifications and training
- **Personal care aides** must complete a DOH-approved home health aide program, or the **40-hour** personal care basic training under 18 NYCRR 505.14(e), before serving clients [S28][S23]. The full program must be finished within 3 months of hire [S23].
- **Home health aides** must complete a basic home health aide training program or an approved equivalency exam [S28].
- **In-service:** 12 hours a year for HHAs and 6 for PCAs [S26]. Medicaid personal care also requires 3 hours semiannually [S23].
- **Before patient contact [S26]:**
  - health assessment, then annually;
  - rubella and measles immunity;
  - TB screening;
  - influenza vaccination, or a mask during flu season;
  - ID verification and reference checks;
  - Home Care Registry entry;
  - CHRC fingerprinting. Temporary employment is allowed pending results, with supervision [S29].
- **Performance evaluations** kept in each personnel record [S26], with in-home supervision as required by 766.5 [S24] and the 90-day Medicaid RN visits [S23].

### Clinical oversight
- RN supervision of aides "as appropriate," plus in-home supervision at initial service and when the client's condition changes. Plans of care are revised as needed [S24].
- **Medicaid personal care** requires an RN supervisory visit **at least every 90 days**. Visits may be combined every six months for stable, self-directing clients [S23].

### Patient rights
Before care starts, give the client written rights, a statement of services and charges, and the complaint process. Report charge changes within 30 days [S27].

### Required systems and reporting
- **EVV** for Medicaid PCS (choice model; data to the State aggregator) [S31].
- **Annual registration** (PHL §3605-b) [S13].
- **Weekly HERDS survey,** including census by licensed county (since June 17, 2025; window Tuesday 8 a.m. to Thursday 2 p.m.) [S43].
- **Cost reports** when DOH requires them (PHL §3612) [S13].
- **Wage parity** annual certification and audited statement for downstate Medicaid work [S17].
sections.market_conditions:
### Supply
- The state limits new entry through the public need presumption. In 2022, 20 counties had 5+ agencies each serving 25+ patients [S5].
- The number of licensed LHCSAs statewide is not published in the sources reviewed.
- MLTC contract caps [S12] and the proposed 2027–2029 moratorium (S4400, not enacted) [S9] show continuing policy pressure to shrink the number of agencies.

### Pricing
- **Medicaid:** the NYC FFS Level II rate is $32.11/hour (January 1, 2024) [S19]. Upstate FFS rates are about $30–$41 [S20]. MLTC rates are negotiated and unpublished.
- **Private pay:** the New York median is $35/hour, 26th among states [S36].

### Wages
**BLS OEWS May 2025, New York [S35]:**
| Role | 25th pct | Median |
|---|---|---|
| Home health and personal care aides | $18.59 | $19.05 |
| Registered nurses | $45.60 | $52.62 |
| Medical and health services managers | $123,170 (annual) | $164,120 (annual) |
| Office supervisors | — | $79,170 (annual) |
| Medical secretaries | — | $47,710 (annual) |

**Legal floors for 2026:**
- General minimum wage: $17.00 NYC/LI/Westchester; $16.00 rest of state [S15].
- Home care aide minimum: $19.65 / $18.65 [S14].
- On January 1, 2027, the general minimum stays flat, but the home care aide minimum rises to $20.00 / $19.00 [S15][S16].
- Parity adds $2.54 (NYC) or $1.67 (LI/Westchester) for Medicaid work [S17].

The May 2025 BLS median ($19.05) is already **below the 2026 downstate home care floor**. Downstate agencies have no wage room below the statute.

### Trends
- **CDPAP consolidation under PPL** in 2025 [S30].
- **Stricter Minimum Needs Requirements** from September 2025 [S30].
- **Annual home care wage-floor increases** through 2027 [S16].
- **Weekly county census reporting** through HERDS [S43].
sections.financial_narrative:
### How the P&L is built
The unit is one **active client**. Capacity is the census the office team is sized for. Default occupancy is **90%**: the share of that census actually billing its hours in a month. This is an operator assumption.

**Revenue per client per month:**
- **MLTC Medicaid client:** 100 hours × **$32.11** = **$3,211**. The rate is an assumption: DOH's NYC FFS Level II rate, effective January 1, 2024 [S19], used as a stand-in for negotiated MLTC rates. Upstate FFS rates run about $30–$41 [S20]. The 100 hours is an operator assumption.
- **Private-pay client:** 60 hours × **$35** = **$2,100** [S36]. The hours are an operator assumption.

**Aide labor** scales with census. Aides are paid 105 hours per 100 billed, allowing 5% for travel and in-service time (operator estimate).
- Upstate Medicaid aides: **$18.65**, the 2026 rest-of-state home care minimum [S14].
- Upstate private-pay aides: **$19.05**, the BLS New York median [S35].
- Downstate private-pay aides: **$19.65** [S14].
- NYC Medicaid aides: **$22.19** parity total compensation ($19.65 + $2.54) [S17].

**RN costs:**
- 16–24 base hours a month for the required director of patient services [S25];
- 0.75–1.0 hour per client per month for assessments and supervision (90-day visits for Medicaid [S23]);
- all at the NY median of $52.62 [S35]. Hours are operator estimates.

**Payroll burden is 20%:**
- employer FICA 7.65% [S38];
- FUTA and NY unemployment insurance about 2.35% of pay (the 2026 NY new-employer UI rate is 4.1% of the taxable wage base [S48]; with high aide turnover the effective cost can exceed 2.35% of pay);
- workers' compensation 5%;
- benefits 5%.

All but FICA are operator estimates.

**Not modeled (conservative):** FFS (and some MLTC contracts) pay separate RN supervision and assessment visit rates (CY2024 upstate examples about $50–$160 per visit [S20]); the model counts none of this revenue. **Overtime:** the model assumes schedules keep aides under 40 hours a week and avoid spread-of-hours pay (operator assumption) [S14].

**Fixed costs:**
- a director at $79,170 [S35], or a $123,170 administrator for 100 NYC clients [S35];
- schedulers at $47,710 per FTE [S35];
- lease, insurance, EVV software [S31], accounting, on-call and marketing (operator estimates);
- for NYC Medicaid, a wage-parity CPA audit [S17] and the MCTMT payroll tax (0.60% of payroll in NYC once quarterly payroll exceeds $437,500) [S47].

**Per-client costs:**
- training, CHRC and health screening;
- PPE;
- mileage: 40 miles × $0.725 upstate [S39], or transit downstate.

### Results at 90% of target census
| Configuration | Net / month | Margin | Break-even clients |
|---|---|---|---|
| Upstate mixed, 80 clients (65% MLTC / 35% private) | **+$25,048** | 12.3% | 34.9 |
| Upstate MLTC Medicaid only, 60 clients | **+$20,403** | 11.8% | 26.4 |
| Upstate private pay only, 40 clients | +$2,262 | 3.0% | 31.9 |
| Downstate private pay only, 40 clients | −$1,067 | −1.4% | 38.0 |
| NYC MLTC Medicaid with wage parity, 100 clients | −$7,055 | −2.4% | 113.0 |

At 80% census, the upstate mixed agency still earns about $19,650 a month and the upstate MLTC agency about $15,970.

### Sensitivity (the MLTC rate is the decisive input)
**MLTC rate:**
| Rate | Upstate MLTC (60 clients) | Upstate mixed (80 clients) | NYC parity (100 clients) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $34.00 | +$30,609 | +$33,893 | +$9,955 |
| $30.00 | +$9,009 | +$15,173 | −$26,045 |
| $28.00 | −$1,791 | +$5,813 | −$44,045 |

Break-even rates at 90% census:
- upstate MLTC agency: about **$28.33/hour**;
- upstate mixed agency: about **$26.76/hour** for the Medicaid share;
- NYC parity agency: about **$32.89/hour**.

**Wage-floor and wage-parity changes:**
- **January 2027 wage floor:** at $19.00 upstate ($19.40 for private-pay aides), the upstate mixed agency falls to +$22,318 and the upstate MLTC agency to +$18,021. At $20.00 downstate, the NYC parity agency falls to −$11,044. These assume rates do not rise with the floor.
- **Long Island / Westchester parity** ($21.32 instead of NYC's $22.19): the 100-client downstate Medicaid agency improves to about +$3,446 (with the Zone 2 MCTMT rate of 0.34% instead of 0.60%) [S47].

**Other inputs:**
- **Hours per Medicaid client:** at 80 authorized hours instead of 100, the upstate MLTC agency earns +$11,103 and the mixed agency +$16,988.
- **Private-pay price:**
  - at $32/hour, the upstate private agency falls to −$4,218;
  - at $38/hour, upstate private earns +$8,742 and downstate private +$5,413;
  - at $40/hour, downstate private earns +$9,733.
- **RN time:** at 1.5 hours per client, the mixed agency earns +$22,320.
- **Workers' comp:** at 8%, the mixed agency earns +$20,875.
- **Payroll tax:** at 11% instead of 10% (higher effective UI cost [S48]), the mixed agency earns +$23,657 and the upstate MLTC agency +$19,201.

### Cash needs
DOH requires documented working capital equal to two months of operating expenses before approval [S6]. The model shows about $45,000–$98,000 based on the first two months of modeled expenses. The real cash need is the ramp-up loss while census builds. At the modeled ramp, the P&L generator computes about **$89,000** for the upstate mixed agency and about **$71,000** for the upstate MLTC agency, plus $40,000–$57,000 of one-time startup costs. That startup figure includes the $2,000 application fee [S3] and legal work on the need rebuttal. Licensing itself can take several PHHPC cycles [S3], so budget pre-opening rent and salaries separately.
sections.risks:
### Regulatory risks
1. **Public need denial.** In a no-need county, PHHPC can propose disapproval on need alone [S2]. The $2,000 fee is not refunded [S3]. All of NYC, Long Island and Westchester were no-need in 2022 [S5].
2. **New moratorium.** S4400 would freeze new LHCSA applications from April 1, 2027 to March 31, 2029 [S9]. It is not law, but the 2018–2020 freeze shows the State uses this tool. File early if you intend to apply.
3. **Medicaid gatekeeping.** PHL §3605-c lets DOH require a contract before any LHCSA enrolls in Medicaid [S10]. It is not implemented as far as found, but it is on the books.
4. **Registration lapse.** An unregistered agency cannot operate or be paid. The penalty is $500 a month, and missing two periods can trigger revocation [S13].

### Payer risks
5. **MLTC contracts.** Plans may cap the number of LHCSAs they contract with [S12], and rates are unpublished. The upstate Medicaid model turns negative below about **$28.33/hour**.
6. **Shrinking eligibility.** The September 2025 Minimum Needs Requirements limit new personal care and MLTC entrants [S30].
7. **Rate lag.** The latest FFS rates are effective January 1, 2024 [S21], while aide floors rose in 2025 and 2026 and rise again in 2027 [S14][S16]. Plan capitation assumes plans pay $0.55 more per hour from January 2026 [S44], but pass-through to the LHCSA rate is negotiated; without pass-through language, each increase cuts margin. The 2027 increase alone costs the upstate mixed agency about $2,700 a month.

### Labor risks
8. **Wage parity compliance.** Downstate Medicaid aides must receive parity total compensation. Willful underpayment is a misdemeanor, and payers may not pay for care by underpaid aides [S17].
9. **Downstate wage squeeze.** The 2026 downstate floor ($19.65) already exceeds the May 2025 BLS median aide wage ($19.05) [S14][S35]. Recruiting above the floor erodes thin margins.
10a. **Overtime and spread-of-hours.** Aides are owed 1½ times their regular rate over 40 hours a week (44 for residential employees) and spread-of-hours pay for workdays over 10 hours, plus call-in pay where applicable [S14]. The model assumes schedules avoid overtime (operator assumption).
10b. **MCTMT.** Downstate agencies with more than $312,500 of quarterly payroll owe the Metropolitan Commuter Transportation Mobility Tax (0.60% of payroll in NYC, 0.34% on Long Island/Westchester at $437,500–$2.5M a quarter) [S47]. The NYC model includes it.
10. **Training and screening throughput.** Required before any client contact [S23][S26][S29]:
    - 40 hours of PCA basic training;
    - health assessments and immunizations;
    - CHRC fingerprinting.

    High turnover multiplies this cost.

### Operating risks
11. **Long pre-revenue period.** DOH publishes no timeline. PHHPC meets only six times a year, and the P&P review and pre-opening survey come after approval [S3]. Rent and salaries before licensure are not in the monthly model.
12. **EVV and documentation.** Visits without EVV data, and lapsed 90-day RN supervision, expose Medicaid claims to denial or recoupment [S31][S23].
sections.recommendations:
### 1. Pick counties before anything else
Build a 5-county service area in **one DOH region** from the **presumed-need list** [S3][S5]. Upstate examples include Oneida, Schenectady, Rensselaer, Niagara, Ontario, Jefferson and St. Lawrence. Email homecareliccert@health.ny.gov [S49] to confirm current county status, because the published list is from 2022 [S5][S43]. Avoid NYC, Long Island and Westchester for a first license unless you have strong rebuttal data or are buying an existing agency.

### 2. Consider buying instead of building downstate
A **change of ownership** of a LHCSA that actively serves **25+ patients** skips public need review [S2][S3]. You may also adopt the seller's approved P&P manual to speed licensure [S3]. This is the realistic way into saturated counties.

### 3. Secure MLTC interest before you file
Before filing, talk with the MLTC plans serving your counties.
- Ask whether their networks are open under the contract caps [S12].
- Ask what hourly rate they pay.
- Treat **$28.33/hour** as the floor for a Medicaid-heavy upstate model.
- Insist on contract language that passes through the January 2027 home care wage increase [S16].
- Letters of support from plans also strengthen a need rebuttal.

### 4. Run a blended book
The best modeled configuration is an **upstate agency with about 80 clients, 65% MLTC and 35% private pay**: about +$25,000 a month at 90% census. Price private care at or above the $35 New York median [S36]. Private pay protects you if plan rates disappoint.

### 5. Budget for the application, not just the opening
- Show working capital of at least two months of expenses, with a CPA review [S6][S3]. Model about $45,000–$98,000.
- Hold about $111,000–$145,000 in total for the upstate configurations (the generator's cash-needed figure) to cover startup costs and ramp losses.
- Add pre-licensure rent if you lease early.

### 6. Build compliance into the launch
Before the pre-opening survey, have these in place:
- a RN director of patient services [S25];
- a quality improvement committee that meets quarterly [S25];
- 40-hour-trained aides [S23];
- registry and CHRC workflows [S26][S29];
- an EVV vendor connected to the State aggregator [S31];
- annual registration [S13];
- HERDS weekly reporting [S43].

Downstate Medicaid work also needs a wage parity payroll setup and a CPA engaged for the annual audited statement [S17].

### 7. Watch S4400
If it moves, file before April 1, 2027 [S9].

checklist.instructions: As of October 2026 there is no moratorium (the 2018–2020 freeze expired 3/31/2020). Check the status of Senate Bill S4400, which would freeze new applications from 4/1/2027 to 3/31/2029.

checklist.task: Check each county against the DOH no-need list
checklist.instructions: On the 2022 list are Albany, Bronx, Broome, Chautauqua, Dutchess, Erie, Kings, Monroe, Nassau, New York, Onondaga, Orange, Putnam, Queens, Richmond, Rockland, Saratoga, Suffolk, Ulster and Westchester. checklist.phase: PHASE 0 — FEASIBILITY: COUNTY NEED & PAYER CHECK
checklist.task: Decide: new license, change of ownership, or affiliated (restricted) license
checklist.instructions: Buying an LHCSA that actively serves 25+ patients avoids public need review. Agencies affiliated with an ALP, PACE, NFP or CCRC are exempt if they serve only that program's patients. Everyone else faces the need test.

checklist.phase: PHASE 0 — FEASIBILITY: COUNTY NEED & PAYER CHECK
checklist.task: If any county is on the no-need list, build a data-driven rebuttal for each one
checklist.instructions: Use the §765-1.16(d) factors: demographics and health status, documented and unduplicated waiting lists, capacity and quality of existing agencies, workforce, training resources, cultural competency and specialty subpopulations. An application missing a required rebuttal may not be accepted.

checklist.phase: PHASE 0 — FEASIBILITY: COUNTY NEED & PAYER CHECK
checklist.task: Commit to serving hard-to-reach groups
checklist.instructions: Every initial applicant must agree to serve people in the county who have trouble getting care because of minority status, age, medical history, case complexity, payment source or location.

checklist.phase: PHASE 0 — FEASIBILITY: COUNTY NEED & PAYER CHECK
checklist.task: Talk to MLTC plans in your counties about network openings and rates
checklist.instructions: Plans may contract with only 1 LHCSA per 100 enrollees downstate or per 60 rest of state, under 2018 DOH guidance. Ask whether they will contract with you and at what hourly rate. The modeled upstate Medicaid agency breaks even at about $28.33/hour.

checklist.phase: PHASE 0 — FEASIBILITY: COUNTY NEED & PAYER CHECK
checklist.task: Decide whether you truly need a license (companion-only vs. personal care)
checklist.instructions: A license is required for nursing, home health aide or personal care services. Personal care includes help with hygiene, dressing, feeding and household tasks essential to health. Get DOH's written view before operating companion-only without a license.

checklist.task: Form a New York LLC (or corporation) with the Department of State
checklist.instructions: Articles of Organization cost $200. Make sure the ownership matches what you will disclose on Schedule 1.

checklist.task: Complete LLC publication within 120 days
checklist.instructions: Publish in two county-designated newspapers for 6 consecutive weeks, then file the Certificate of Publication ($50) with both affidavits. Missing the deadline suspends the LLC's authority to do business.

checklist.task: Obtain an EIN
checklist.instructions: Free from the IRS; issued online immediately.

checklist.task: Obtain an organizational (Type 2) NPI
checklist.instructions: Free in NPPES. Needed for Medicaid enrollment and MLTC contracting.

checklist.task: Confirm at least one principal has health care experience
checklist.instructions: DOH-1056A requires at least one principal (shareholder, member, partner, board member or proprietor) with health care experience, shown in the Affirmative Statement of Qualifications.

checklist.task: List every principal and controlling person, plus all health facilities they have controlled
checklist.instructions: Disclose all U.S. health care, adult care or mental health facilities controlled or operated, with dates and any penalties, suspensions or revocations.

checklist.task: Gather organizational documents for the application
checklist.instructions: Bylaws, certificate of incorporation or articles, operating or partnership agreements, any assumed-name certificate, and a board resolution authorizing the application (corporations).

checklist.task: Open a business bank account and fund working capital
checklist.instructions: Working capital must be on hand or committed (awarded loans/grants) at filing. Prospective funding does not count.

checklist.task: Get NYSE-CON access and download the current LHCSA application
checklist.instructions: File electronically through NYSE-CON. Process questions: cons@health.ny.gov. Technical issues: nysecon@health.ny.gov. Use the post-2022 form; older forms are not accepted.

checklist.task: Prepare the financial feasibility package
checklist.instructions: Show working capital of at least two months of estimated operating expenses. Include a funding plan, projected expenses (year 1 and year 3), a balance sheet if using existing funds, personal financial statements for equity contributors, and revenue that covers expenses over time.

checklist.task: Engage a CPA to review and confirm working capital
checklist.instructions: DOH requires CPA review of the funding. The applicant pays the CPA's fee.

checklist.task: Complete Schedule 1 for every principal
checklist.instructions: Schedule 1 is the disclosure form with the Affirmative Statement of Qualifications, reviewed for character, experience and competence.

checklist.task: Attach the public need narrative and any rebuttals
checklist.instructions: One rebuttal for each no-need county, plus the access commitment.

checklist.task: Submit in NYSE-CON and mail the $2,000 fee within 30 days
checklist.instructions: Make the check payable to the NYS Department of Health and write the NYSE-CON submission number on it. The fee is nonrefundable once the application is acknowledged, including if PHHPC disapproves.

checklist.task: Answer DOH requests for information quickly
checklist.instructions: Applications are reviewed in order of acknowledgment. 'Under Review' applications may get information requests through NYSE-CON. Slow answers delay your PHHPC slot.

checklist.task: Track the PHHPC agenda
checklist.instructions: PHHPC meets six times a year and may approve, contingently approve or disapprove. It can propose disapproval on need alone; you may request a hearing.

checklist.task: Report material changes while the application is pending
checklist.instructions: Significant changes in principals, capacity, operating budget or service area are amendments needing approval. Nondisclosure can void an approval.

checklist.task: Write the Policy & Procedure Manual and submit it to the regional office after contingent approval
checklist.instructions: Cover patient rights, plan of care and supervision, governing authority, QI, complaints, emergency plan, personnel and infection control. The regional office must accept it before the pre-opening survey.
checklist.cite: DOH LHCSA FAQ A.Q3; 10 NYCRR Part 766

checklist.task: Hire the RN who directs and supervises patient care
checklist.instructions: Every LHCSA must employ at least one licensed, currently registered professional nurse.

checklist.task: Lease an adequately sized office
checklist.instructions: The governing authority must provide an adequately sized office with access to patient records. Lease cost is an operator estimate; verify locally.

checklist.task: Seat the quality improvement committee
checklist.instructions: Include a consumer and health professionals. Meet at least 4 times a year, review policies and a sample of records, and report in writing to the governing authority.

checklist.task: Set up the complaint log and process
checklist.instructions: Respond in writing within 15 days. Appeals go to the governing authority within 30 days. Tell patients they may complain to DOH.

checklist.task: Adopt the patient rights notice and statement of charges
checklist.instructions: Give them in writing before care starts. Disclose third-party coverage and patient liability, and report changes within 30 days.

checklist.task: Write the emergency/continuity plan and list 24-hour contacts in the HPN directory
checklist.instructions: Review the coverage policy annually and update the directory monthly.

checklist.task: Hire aides with approved training only
checklist.instructions: PCAs need a DOH-approved HHA program or the 40-hour PCA basic training (finished within 3 months of hire, and before services). HHAs need an approved basic program or equivalency exam.

checklist.task: Run CHRC fingerprinting for every prospective employee
checklist.instructions: Submit the signed form and two fingerprint sets within 10 business days of printing. Two IDs are required, one with a photo. Temporary employment is allowed pending results, with supervision.

checklist.task: Enter every aide in the Home Care Worker Registry
checklist.instructions: Required before or at hire.

checklist.instructions: Health assessment, rubella and measles immunity, TB screening, and flu vaccination or a mask during flu season. Repeat the health assessment annually for staff with patient contact.

checklist.instructions: Required for all personnel.

checklist.instructions: 12 hours a year for HHAs and 6 for PCAs. Medicaid personal care adds 3 hours semiannually.

checklist.task: Screen referrals against the 2025 Minimum Needs Requirements

checklist.task: Set private-pay prices from the local market
checklist.instructions: The New York median is $35/hour for non-medical in-home care. The upstate private-only model loses money at $32.

checklist.instructions: MLTC care managers, hospital and rehab discharge planners, physicians, elder law attorneys and senior centers. Former CDPAP consumers who want an agency are another source.

checklist.instructions: Use written admission criteria.

checklist.task: RN assessment and plan of care for each new client; supervise the aide on the first visit when required

checklist.task: Track occupancy and hours delivered versus authorized
checklist.instructions: The P&L assumes 90% of target census billing each month (operator assumption).

checklist.task: Submit the weekly HERDS survey with census by licensed county
checklist.instructions: Window opens Tuesday 8:00 a.m. and closes Thursday 2:00 p.m. (since 6/17/2025). Contact hcstatrpts@health.ny.gov.

checklist.task: Renew registration every year
checklist.instructions: Missing periods leads to fines and possible revocation.

checklist.task: Hold quarterly QI committee meetings and document findings
checklist.instructions: At least 4 times a year.

checklist.task: Do annual health assessments, TB screening, flu documentation and performance evaluations
checklist.instructions: Keep performance evaluations in each personnel record (766.11) and do in-home supervision as required by 766.5 and the 90-day Medicaid RN visits (18 NYCRR 505.14).

checklist.task: File cost reports when DOH requires them
checklist.instructions: Filed within 90 days of notice; a 30-day correction window applies.

checklist.task: Update pay for each January home care wage increase
checklist.instructions: 1/1/2027: $20.00 / $19.00. Check whether MLTC contracts pass the increase through.

checklist.task: Wage parity annual certification and audit (downstate Medicaid)
checklist.instructions: File the certification each year with the independently audited statement.

checklist.task: Request administrative amendments to add counties, services or sites
checklist.instructions: Contact the regional office or homecareapplications@health.ny.gov. New counties are still subject to the need rule.

checklist.task: Get approval before any ownership change or management contract
checklist.instructions: A change of ownership needs a new CON application, and the license is not transferable. Management contracts need commissioner approval 60 days before they take effect.

corrections_vs_previous: No New York Personal Home Care bundle was found in Drive (read-only search, October 13, 2026). The closest prior file, 'New_York_Home_health_agencies_Licensing_Checklist.xlsx' (generated 2026-01-21), was reviewed. It is not reused, and these errors were found.

The old checklist never mentions the public need test. Since April 1, 2020, every new LHCSA must prove public need. There is a presumption of no need in counties with 5+ LHCSAs each serving 25+ patients, and a rebuttal is mandatory there or the application may not be accepted [S2][S3][S5]. This is the single biggest factor in whether a license is granted.

It omits the PHHPC approval step and gets the sequence wrong. The P&P manual is submitted after PHHPC contingent approval, followed by a pre-opening survey [S3]. It also tells applicants to print 4 hard copies; filing is electronic through NYSE-CON [S3].

It omits the required working capital (two months of operating expenses, CPA-confirmed) [S6][S3], annual registration under PHL §3605-b [S13], the home care aide minimum wage and wage parity [S14][S17], EVV [S31], and the 5-county / one-region limit [S3].

It cites the wrong rules. '10 NYCRR §765-2.1' for agency type, '766.5' for personnel and '766.11' for QA are wrong. Personnel is §766.11 and quality improvement is in §766.9 [S26][S25]. It also adds fire-marshal, certificate-of-occupancy and environmental inspections, which DOH does not require for LHCSA licensure.

It includes Medicaid recipient asset limits, which do not apply to licensing an agency. It labels the Staff Exclusion List a 'Health Homes' check and gives unsourced fees ($101.45 CHRC, $25 SCR); these were not carried over.
